newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Archbishop sets conditions for pivotal Zaire job.
newsitem.headline: Archbishop sets conditions for pivotal Zaire job.

text.p: Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo, touted by some as the key to peace in Zaire, said on Sunday he must have certain guarantees if he is to take back his old job as speaker of the transitional parliament.

Some diplomats and politicians say the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Kisangani, which was captured by Laurent Kabila's rebels on March 15, could step in and provide embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko with a dignified exit.

Others say that with the rebels threatening to attack the capital Kinshasa if Mobutu does not stand down, Monsengwo could act as a national mediator -- a role he previously played as speaker until he was ousted in July 1995.

"I will only accept if I have national and international guarantees," he told a news conference in Belgium during a stopover on his way back to Kinshasa from the Vatican where he attended a conference. He did not elaborate.
Supporters of Mobutu, who has cancer, voted on Saturday to restore Monsengwo as speaker -- the constitutional successor to the president in the event of death or incapacity.
The radical opposition of Etienne Tshisekedi, the other main political force in Kinshasa, walked out before the "consensus" vote -- raising doubts as to whether it was binding.
The rebels, who took up arms in October and control three-quarters of Zaire, insist Mobutu must stand down and hand power to Kabila.
Monsengwo, who is still popular in a country with a Roman Catholic majority, held the job of speaker at the height of Zaire's transition to democracy.

An alliance of Mobutu supporters, fearing his popularity in the event of elections, joined forces with Tshisekedi supporters to oust him in July 1995. Tshisekedi supporters dismiss Monsengwo is "Mobutist".
Mobutu returned to Kinshasa on Saturday but he and Kabila have agreed to a second round of face-to-face talks chaired by South Africa's Nelson Mandela on board a South African navy ship on Wednesday.
The first such meeting, on May 4, ended with Mobutu offering to hand power to an elected successor and Kabila demanding that he stand down immediately.

Kabila said in a French television interview on Saturday he had agreed to meet Mobutu for talks, but ruled out calling off his military drive which has reached to less than 200 km (125 miles) from the teeming capital of five million.
"No one has officially asked me to stop my offensive. We shall continue," Kabila said.
Mobutu and several other French-speaking African leaders, meeting on Thursday, proposed a stronger role for parliament in solving Zaire's crisis and called for a new speaker.
Mobutu supporters see a key role for Monsengwo.

"He is not an alternative to either President Mobutu or Kabila," Christophe Lutundula, second deputy speaker of parliament, told Reuters. "We are hoping he will play a role as a national mediator and will persuade all sides to agree on a way of safeguarding the democratic process in Zaire."
Mobutu, 66, has dominated the mineral-rich country at the heart of Africa for over three decades.
His most enduring Western ally, France, welcomed Monsengwo's election, saying it could help an orderly transfer of power.

On the humanitarian front, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said in Japan the plight of Rwandan Hutu refugees in rebel-held Zaire was "extremely distressing" and that the U.N. was working to ensure rebel cooperation with their repatriation.
